turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic? What's been concerning you?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, hey doc. Thanks for seeing me. Um, well, what brings me in is... work's just getting really bad lately. I'm a construction manager, and I'll start a safety briefing with the guys, or sit down for a plan review, and I'll be trying really, really hard to just pay attention to the paper in front of me. But within minutes, my mind is just... it's off on three other job problems. 

Like yesterday, we had this issue with the concrete pour on the south elevation. The subcontractor we hired, Jimmy's crew, they always show up late. I swear, every single time I use Jimmy, it's a massive headache. His brother used to run the crew and they were great, but he moved to Texas a couple of years ago. Austin, I think? Supposedly the market down there is booming, but the heat would kill me. 

Anyway, what was I... right, the briefings. So I'll be in the middle of a plan review, and my head is just miles away worrying about Jimmy's guys or a lumber delivery, and I end up missing things in the blueprints that I absolutely know I should have caught. It's getting to be a real liability.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient reports making careless mistakes by missing details in blueprints that he knows he should have caught.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes difficulty sustaining attention during safety briefings and plan reviews, noting his mind wanders within minutes.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient is easily distracted by unrelated thoughts about other job problems and demonstrates this distractibility by going off on a tangent during the conversation.

turns.doctor_question: When your mind wanders during these meetings, are you getting pulled away by worries about things that might go wrong—like the concrete quality or Jimmy not showing up—or does your attention just kind of drift off on its own, even when you're not particularly worried about anything?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it's... it's a bit of both, honestly. Sometimes I'm definitely worrying about Jimmy's guys, because like I said, they're a disaster waiting to happen. But other times, it's just... I don't know, my brain just changes the channel. Like, I'll be looking at a structural drawing, and suddenly I'm thinking about how I need to change the oil in my truck. Which reminds me, I really need to get that done before the weekend because I promised my wife we'd drive up to the lake. We've got this little cabin up there, needs a new roof actually. I was thinking of putting metal up this time, you know, lasts longer, better for the snow load. The guy next door to us did shingles last year and they're already curling. 

Wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, the wandering. Yeah, so it's not always worrying. Sometimes I just completely drift off into whatever random thought pops in there, and I don't even realize I've stopped paying attention to the meeting until someone asks me a question and I have no idea what they just said.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes losing focus and stopping paying attention during meetings and while looking at drawings.
symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient admits that when someone asks a question during a meeting, they often have no idea what was just said.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly states they get distracted by unrelated, random thoughts popping into their head.
symptom_reasoning.S056: The patient confirms they experience worry about work issues, such as Jimmy's crew being a 'disaster waiting to happen'.

turns.doctor_question: Besides work meetings, do you notice this same problem with paying attention in other situations—like when you're reading at home, watching TV, or having conversations with your wife or friends?
turns.patient_response:
Oh yeah, all the time. It’s actually causing some friction at home. Like, my wife or my foreman will be talking straight to me, and I’m looking right at them, making eye contact and everything. But then my brain just checks out, and I have to stop them and say, "Hey, run that by me again," because I only caught the last few words. 

It drives my wife absolutely nuts. Just the other night she was telling me something about... I think it was the dog’s vet appointment? We have this golden retriever, Buster. Great dog, but he’s got this weird allergy thing going on with his paws right now. He just chews on them all night long, makes this awful slurping sound. The vet gave us this special medicated shampoo, cost like forty bucks for a tiny little bottle, which is just a total rip-off if you ask me. I mean, it smells exactly like oatmeal, I could probably just soak his feet in Quaker Oats for a fraction of the price, right? My buddy Dave did that with his lab and it cleared right up, though Dave's kind of cheap like that. He actually tried to fix his own transmission once and ended up leaving the truck on blocks in his driveway for six months. 

Wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, paying attention to stuff. But yeah, conversations are tough. I'll be looking right at someone and just not hearing a single thing they said.

symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient explicitly states that when his wife or foreman speak directly to him, his brain 'checks out' and he fails to hear what they are saying.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates being easily distracted by unrelated thoughts during the interview, going on a long tangent about his dog and friend before forgetting the original topic of conversation.

turns.doctor_question: Going back to when you were in school—elementary, middle, high school—did you have these same kinds of problems paying attention in class, or is this something that's really only started happening in recent years?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, no, it's definitely not a recent thing. Man, back in elementary school, it was already a whole issue. My teachers were constantly telling my parents that I couldn’t stay in my seat, or that I always talked out of turn. I was always losing my homework, too. And I'd just rush through the directions on assignments before I even really understood what we were supposed to be doing. Just trying to get it over with, you know? 

I remember my fourth-grade teacher, Mrs. Higgins. She was this tiny little lady, but she was incredibly strict. She used to make us go outside and clap the chalkboard erasers against the brick wall if we acted up. Man, the amount of chalk dust you'd inhale doing that... you could never get away with that today. OSHA would be all over it. We actually just had a safety inspector on my site last Tuesday checking our silica dust protocols because we were doing some heavy masonry cutting. Those guys can slap you with a massive fine if your crew isn't wearing the right respirators. I had to buy a whole new case of N95 masks for the guys, which are crazy expensive right now because the supply chain from our main distributor is still completely backed up. My rep over there, Tony, he says it's because of some shipping container shortage out on the West Coast, but I honestly think he's just upcharging us because he knows we need them for the city contract. Tony’s always been a bit of a shark like that. We used to play softball together in this rec league, and he'd argue with the ump over every single call...

Wait, sorry, I'm doing it again, aren't I? You asked about school. But yeah, to answer your question, it's not new. The teachers were on my case about all that stuff since I was a little kid.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient describes rushing through assignment directions without understanding them, indicating a failure to give close attention to details.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient admits to rushing through directions and not properly following what they were supposed to be doing on assignments.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly states they were 'always losing my homework' in school.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates being easily distracted by unrelated thoughts, going on a long tangent about OSHA, masks, and a softball league before catching themselves.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient notes that teachers complained they 'couldn't stay in my seat' during class.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient mentions that they 'always talked out of turn' in class, indicating interrupting or intruding on others.

turns.doctor_question: When you were in elementary school and your teachers said you couldn't stay in your seat, what exactly were you doing? Were you getting up and walking around the classroom, or were you fidgeting and squirming in your seat?
turns.patient_response:
Well, back then it was definitely getting up and walking around. I'd just get out of my desk and walk over to the pencil sharpener, or go look out the window. And honestly, it hasn't really changed. I still do the exact same thing now. Like, we have these long progress meetings, right? And where everybody else can just sit through the whole thing, I’m always the guy standing up. I'll walk over to get coffee, or I'll step outside to check something, basically just making up any excuse to move around. 

Speaking of the coffee, we actually just got one of those fancy Keurig machines for the job trailer. The guys were complaining about the old drip pot tasting like burnt motor oil, which, fair enough, it did. But now everyone's fighting over the little pods. We had this whole blowout yesterday because Jimmy's drywall crew drank all the dark roast and left nothing but decaf. Who drinks decaf on a construction site? It makes absolutely no sense. You need the caffeine to keep up with the schedule, especially since we're already three weeks behind on the framing. The lumber yard sent us a whole bunk of bowed studs last week, and I had to spend half the day on the phone with the supplier trying to get them swapped out. The guy on the phone had the nerve to tell me wood is a natural product and some warping is expected. I told him I've been in this business twenty years and I know the difference between a natural warp and a piece of wood shaped like a banana...

Wait, sorry. The seat thing. Yeah, I was definitely a walker. Still am, really. Just can't stay glued to a chair.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly confirms a history and current pattern of leaving his seat when expected to remain seated, such as getting up during long meetings to get coffee or check on things.

turns.doctor_question: Besides the fidgeting and getting up from your seat, do you find yourself doing things without thinking them through first? Like interrupting people, making quick decisions you later regret, or acting on impulses?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, the interrupting thing... that's a big one. I do it all the time at work. Like, I’ll just walk right up on two subcontractors who are clearly in the middle of talking, or I'll see one of the guys trying to work through some paperwork, and I just jump right in with my own point before anyone even asks me. I just blurt it out. And I know it rubs people the wrong way, but it's like the thought is in my head and it just has to come out right that second. 

It actually caused a huge blowup with my electrical sub, Mike, a couple weeks ago. Mike's a good guy, does great work, but he's incredibly particular about how he runs his conduit. He was trying to explain this whole rerouting issue to his apprentice, and I just barged in and told them to run it through the drop ceiling instead. Mike got so mad his face turned purple. He drives this massive Ford F-250, lifted, with the dual exhaust—loudest truck you've ever heard. He actually backed it right into the port-a-john last summer because he couldn't see over the tailgate. Thankfully nobody was in it, but man, the smell... we had to get the sanitation company out there same-day for an emergency cleanup. Cost me a fortune. The guy they sent out was this kid, maybe nineteen, looked absolutely miserable the whole time he was hosing it down. I don't blame him, honestly. I tried to tip him a twenty, but he wouldn't take it. Said it was against company policy. Which is crazy to me, right? Like, if a kid is cleaning up a knocked-over port-a-john, let him take the twenty bucks. 

But anyway, yeah. I interrupt people constantly. I just can't seem to hold the thought in my head and wait my turn.

symptom_reasoning.S017: The patient explicitly states they cannot hold a thought in their head and 'wait my turn'.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient admits to constantly interrupting people and jumping into conversations uninvited.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, going off on a long, unrelated story about a subcontractor's truck, a port-a-john, and a sanitation worker before returning to the original topic.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever made impulsive decisions about money—like spending a lot without thinking it through—or done anything risky like speeding, reckless driving, or substance use that got you into real trouble?
turns.patient_response:
I mean, not really? Like, I don't think I'm out there blowing my life savings or driving like a maniac or anything. I'm actually pretty careful with the big stuff. Especially driving, because I've got the company truck, you know? It's a Chevy Silverado, 2500, heavy duty. Great truck, honestly. Tows like a dream. We had to haul this massive skid steer out to a site in the county last month, and it didn't even struggle on those steep grades. The only thing I hate about it is the gas mileage. I'm practically living at the pump. And gas prices right now, man, they're just completely out of control. I was talking to the guy at the Sunoco down the street—he's this older guy, always wears a fishing hat, nice guy—and he was saying they're supposed to go up another twenty cents by Memorial Day. It's ridiculous. It really cuts into our overhead, especially when we're running back and forth to the supply house three times a day because somebody forgot to order enough fasteners. I swear, I have to micromanage everything on these jobs just to keep us in the black...

But, uh, what were you asking? Oh, right, money and risky stuff. No, I don't really do anything crazy like that. I'm pretty standard there, I guess.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient loses track of the doctor's question because they become distracted by their own unrelated thoughts about their truck, gas prices, and work.
symptom_reasoning.S041: The patient explicitly denies making impulsive decisions about money or blowing their life savings.
symptom_reasoning.S078: The patient explicitly denies driving like a maniac or engaging in other risky, crazy behaviors.

turns.doctor_question: How long would you say you've been having these problems with attention, fidgeting, and interrupting—are we talking months, or has this been going on for years? And has it actually caused you real problems at work or at home, or is it more just an annoyance?
turns.patient_response:
Well, the problems at work... it's been really bad for about two years and two months now. That's when they completely overhauled the construction schedule on us and the hours just went totally chaotic. Before that, things were a little more predictable, you know? But then corporate brought in this new project management software. Procore, I think it's called. They swore up and down it was going to streamline everything, make us all more efficient. We had to sit through this three-day training seminar at the Marriott downtown just to learn how to use the stupid thing. The catering at that hotel, by the way, was terrible. They served these rubbery chicken breasts and steamed broccoli that tasted like it had been sitting in a warmer since the Bush administration. I actually snuck out the side door on the second day and walked three blocks to get a decent Italian sub from this little deli I know. Best pastrami in the city, hands down. The owner, Sal, he's been there for like thirty years. Used to be a bricklayer before he opened the shop, so we always talk shop when I go in. He was telling me about how hard it is to find good mortar guys these days, and I was like, Sal, you're telling me! I had a mason last month who couldn't lay a straight line if his life depended on it. We had to tear down a whole retaining wall and start over...

Anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right. The schedule. Yeah, ever since that changed about two years ago, it's just been a nightmare trying to keep everything straight in my head. It's definitely causing real problems for me on the job.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient describes having a 'nightmare trying to keep everything straight in my head' regarding their work schedule, indicating difficulty organizing tasks.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates being easily distracted by unrelated thoughts, getting sidetracked by memories of software, hotel catering, and a deli owner.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's response exhibits marked tangentiality, wandering through multiple unrelated topics before finally returning to the original question.
symptom_reasoning.S059: The patient loses their train of thought mid-response, asking 'Anyway, what was I saying?', which indicates their mind went blank or they could not sustain attention on the topic.

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned things got really bad about two years ago when the schedule changed. But going back further—before that software and the chaos started—were you already having trouble paying attention and staying focused, or did that really start when everything got hectic?
turns.patient_response:
Well, no, it wasn't just when the schedule changed. I mean, it's always been there, honestly. Like, going way back. My mom used to keep all my old report cards in this big plastic tub in the basement—one of those heavy-duty Rubbermaid ones with the latching lid. Great tubs, by the way. We use them on site for storing smaller hand tools so they don't walk off overnight. You'd be amazed how fast a good DeWalt drill can disappear if you don't lock it up. I actually started spray-painting all my personal tools neon pink just to deter the guys from swiping them. It works, too! Nobody wants to be seen on a job site holding a hot pink circular saw. My framing guy, Dave, he laughed at me for it, but guess whose saw didn't go missing last month? Dave's a piece of work, though. He's got this old hound dog that he brings to the site sometimes, just lets it wander around in the dirt. Dog's name is Buster. Sweetest thing, but he'll eat anything. He got into somebody's lunch cooler a few weeks ago and ate an entire family-size bag of Doritos. Cool Ranch, I think. Dave had to take him to the vet because the dog was throwing up orange foam all afternoon... 

But yeah, the report cards. I was looking through them a while back, and it's the same stuff on every single one, all the way back to elementary school. The teachers were always writing notes to my parents saying I couldn't stay in my seat, I was always talking out of turn, losing my homework. And the directions... I always rushed through them before I even knew what I was supposed to be doing. So, yeah, it's not a new thing. It just got way worse with the new schedule.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient notes they always rushed through directions before knowing what they were supposed to be doing, indicating difficulty following through on instructions.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly mentions a history of 'losing my homework'.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility by unrelated thoughts, getting sidetracked by the mention of a plastic tub into a long story about tools and a dog.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient recalls teachers writing notes that they 'couldn't stay in my seat'.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient mentions a history of 'talking out of turn', which aligns with interrupting or intruding on others.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's response exhibits tangentiality, wandering off-topic to discuss job site tools, a coworker, and a dog eating Doritos before returning to the original point.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever been diagnosed with ADHD or attention deficit disorder, either as a kid or as an adult? And have you ever been prescribed any medications like Ritalin, Adderall, or anything like that to help with focus or attention?
turns.patient_response:
No, never. I mean, nobody ever said anything about a diagnosis when I was a kid. Back then, they just thought you were a bad kid, you know? Or just full of energy. My dad used to say I just needed to run it out. He'd make me do laps around the yard if I was getting too rowdy in the house. We had this huge yard, maybe an acre and a half, backed right up to the woods. It was mostly oak trees and a few maples. In the fall, the leaves were an absolute nightmare. We had this old riding mower, a John Deere, one of the green and yellow ones with the metal bagging attachment on the back. You had to empty that thing every ten minutes or it would clog up the chute. And if the leaves were even a little bit wet from the morning dew? Forget it. You'd spend half the day just unclogging the mower deck with a stick. I actually found this trick later on where if you spray the underside of the deck with WD-40 or silicone spray before you start, the grass and leaves don't stick nearly as bad. It's a lifesaver. I still use that trick on my push mower at home now. It's a Honda, self-propelled. Great engine. Starts on the first pull every single time, even after sitting in the shed all winter. I always make sure to put a little fuel stabilizer in the gas tank before I put it away for the season, though. Ethanol gas these days just wrecks the carburetors if you let it sit...

But no, to answer your question, no doctor ever told me I had anything like that, and I've never taken any of those pills you mentioned. Never had a prescription for anything like that in my life.

symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient provides a highly verbose and unnecessarily detailed tangent about yard work and lawnmowers in response to a simple yes/no question, demonstrating excessive talking in real time.

turns.doctor_question: When you look back at those report cards and what your teachers were saying—about not staying in your seat, talking out of turn, losing homework—do you remember how old you were when that all started? Was it in first grade, kindergarten, or even earlier?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I mean, it was definitely going on in elementary school. Like, first grade, second grade, all of that. The teachers were always telling my parents the same things—couldn't stay in my seat, talking out of turn, losing my homework, rushing through the directions before I even knew what I was supposed to be doing. I actually remember my second-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable. She had this huge beehive hairdo that looked like it was sprayed with industrial lacquer. I swear that thing didn't move an inch, even when she was yelling at us. She kept this jar of jelly beans on her desk, supposedly as a reward for good behavior, but I don't think I ever got a single one. They were the cheap kind, anyway, the ones where the black licorice ones outnumber all the good flavors. I hate black licorice. Reminds me of Jagermeister. I had a buddy in my twenties, Mike, who used to bring a bottle of Jager to every party. We’d do these awful shots called "liquid asphalt" or something. Mike ended up moving out west, Arizona I think. Bought a house out in the desert. He says the dry heat is great, but honestly, I don't know how anyone deals with the scorpions. He sent me a picture once of this giant hairy scorpion just sitting in his bathroom sink... 

But yeah, I'd say it started way back then, kindergarten or first grade. It's just always been how I am.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient describes 'rushing through the directions before I even knew what I was supposed to be doing,' indicating a failure to follow through on instructions.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly recalls a history of 'losing my homework' during elementary school.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates being easily distracted by unrelated thoughts, going on a long tangent about jelly beans, alcohol, and scorpions.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient confirms that teachers frequently complained they 'couldn't stay in my seat.'
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient mentions that they were often reprimanded for 'talking out of turn,' which aligns with interrupting or intruding.
